notes: Slot 18 = UPS (Senghor), de facto single party, using the MD PS sprite (same organization, renamed 1976). There was no real coalition partner; slot 19 holds the underground Maoist milieu. Pro-Soviet PAI placed in slot 4 (popularity). Mourides in 10, Tijaniyya in 14, UCM (Brotherhood-type reformists) in 12.

0.name: Le Réseau Foccart
0.text:
The Foccart network is the web of French advisers, intelligence officers and businessmen that ties Senegal to the Élysée through Jacques Foccart, secretary-general for African affairs under de Gaulle and now Pompidou. In Dakar its pillars are the French troops at Ouakam, the French technical assistants in every ministry and the powerful French-born minister Jean Collin.

The network wants Senghor's regime kept firmly in the Western camp: the franc zone, the defence accords, French firms and a hard line against communists and student agitators. It holds no seats, but in a crisis its security services, money and military guarantee can decide who stays in power.

1.name: Les Originaires des Quatre Communes
1.text:
The originaires are the old citizen families of Dakar, Gorée, Rufisque and Saint-Louis, whose inhabitants held French citizenship long before the rest of the colony. They formed the electorate of Blaise Diagne and Lamine Guèye, whose death in 1968 left their networks without a champion inside the ruling party.

Catholic and Muslim, Wolof and métis alike, they defend French-style legal order, parliamentary traditions, private property and close ties with France and the West. Their influence lies in the bar, the civil service, the municipal councils and the commercial bourgeoisie of the coast, from which they quietly press the UPS for a more liberal course.

2.name: Les Libéraux du Barreau
2.text:
Dakar's lawyers and law faculty form a small but articulate liberal milieu around figures such as the advocate and economist Abdoulaye Wade, a professor at the University of Dakar. They chafe under the de facto single-party system that has reigned since the opposition was absorbed or banned in the mid-1960s.

They call for a legal multi-party opposition, an independent judiciary and a market economy with room for African entrepreneurs rather than state monopolies. Pro-Western but critical of French paternalism, they appeal to the educated urban middle class, and their leverage lies in legal expertise, their pens and the regime's need for a respectable democratic façade.

3.name: Union Nationale des Travailleurs du Sénégal
3.native_full: Union Nationale des Travailleurs du Sénégal
3.text:
The National Union of Senegalese Workers is the main trade-union federation, founded in 1962 as a partner of the ruling party. Its militant base broke with that role in May 1968, when it joined the students in a general strike that shook the regime, and further strikes followed in 1969.

The UNTS demands higher wages, the Africanization of jobs and a say in economic decisions still dominated by French capital. Many of its leaders now seek reconciliation with Senghor through 'responsible participation', but the railway, dock and public-sector unions remain combative, and their ability to paralyse Dakar is the workers' main leverage.

4.name: Parti Africain de l'Indépendance
4.text:
The African Independence Party, founded in Thiès in 1957 by Majhemout Diop, was the first party in French West Africa to demand immediate independence on a Marxist-Leninist programme. Banned since the Saint-Louis election riots of 1960, it survives underground and in exile, weakened by repression and internal splits.

The PAI looks to the Soviet Union as model and patron, seeks the end of French military and economic control, and calls for nationalization and a state of workers and peasants. Its cadres are teachers, students and trade unionists, and its leverage lies in its influence inside the unions and the student movement.

5.name: La Génération de Mai
5.text:
The May generation are the students of the University of Dakar who in May 1968 launched the strike that, joined by the unions, brought Senghor's regime close to collapse and led him to call in the army. Their associations were dissolved and leaders arrested, but radical student committees continue to organize.

Influenced by Maoism, Trotskyism, Fanon and the French May, they denounce neo-colonialism, the French military presence and the UPS monopoly, and demand an African university and revolutionary change. Their leverage lies in their capacity to shut down the campus and the lycées and to spark wider unrest in Dakar.

6.name: Les Disciples de Cheikh Anta
6.text:
Around the historian and physicist Cheikh Anta Diop gathers a network of intellectuals and former activists of his banned parties, the Bloc des Masses Sénégalaises and the Front National Sénégalais. Barred from politics since the mid-1960s, Diop works at the IFAN institute in Dakar, where his radiocarbon laboratory and writings on Africa's past make him a symbol of cultural resistance.

Their creed is a proud African nationalism: the rehabilitation of African civilization, national languages, a federal united Africa and a rejection of Senghor's French-oriented Négritude. Hostile to Western tutelage, they appeal to teachers, students and the Wolof-speaking youth of the towns.

7.name: Les Fidèles de Mamadou Dia
7.text:
Mamadou Dia, Senghor's former prime minister, has been imprisoned at Kédougou since 1963 after the 1962 crisis in which he was accused of attempting a coup. A network of loyal former ministers, cooperative officials and rural militants still regards him as the true architect of Senegalese socialism and campaigns for his release.

Dia's followers want a powerful developmental state that breaks the hold of French trading houses and marabouts over the peasantry through cooperatives and rural animation. Impatient with parliamentary niceties and sceptical of the Western alliance, they favour strong central authority and closer ties with the progressive non-aligned states.

8.name: La Communauté chiite de Dakar
8.text:
Dakar's Lebanese community, largely Shia from southern Lebanon, dominates much of the wholesale and retail trade of the groundnut basin. In 1969 the young cleric Abdul Monem al-Zein arrived from Lebanon, sent with the blessing of Imam Musa al-Sadr, to organize the community's religious life.

The community favours a reformist, socially active Shia Islam centred on education, charity and good relations with the Senegalese state and the Sufi orders. It avoids open politics, but its commercial wealth, links to Beirut and growing religious institutions give it quiet influence with officials who depend on Lebanese credit and trade.

9.name: Le Cercle de Nadjaf
9.text:
A few young Lebanese Shia in Dakar and Kaolack, some educated in the seminaries of Najaf, follow the lectures of the exiled Iranian cleric Ruhollah Khomeini on government by the Islamic jurist. They meet in private homes and circulate recordings and pamphlets from Iraq and Lebanon.

The circle sees both Western capitalism and Soviet communism as enemies of Islam and hopes for revolutionary clerical rule across the Muslim world. Within Senegal it has no political ambitions and few members, but its network along the West African Lebanese trading diaspora could carry radical ideas far beyond its size.

10.name: Confrérie mouride
10.text:
The Mouride Brotherhood, founded by Cheikh Amadou Bamba in the late nineteenth century, is Senegal's most powerful Sufi order, with its holy city at Touba. Since 1968 it has been led by Khalife-General Abdoul Ahad Mbacké, who is expanding Touba and asserting the order's independence from the state.

The Mourides preach work as a form of worship and organize hundreds of thousands of disciples in the groundnut basin under their marabouts. They support the government in exchange for credit, land and respect for their authority, and the khalife's word can deliver votes, keep the countryside calm and make or break any regime.

11.name: Les Arabisants d'Al-Azhar
11.text:
A small group of young Senegalese scholars who studied at Al-Azhar in Cairo and other Arab universities has returned home to find their Arabic diplomas worthless in a French-speaking state. Disillusioned with both the Sufi marabouts and the secular elite, some have embraced the ideas of revolutionary pan-Islamic movements.

They call for the abolition of the secular republic and the unity of all Muslims under a restored caliphate governed by sharia. Without organization or funds, they preach in neighbourhood mosques and Koranic schools of Dakar and Kaolack, and their appeal lies in the frustration of the Arabic-educated who are shut out of jobs and power.

12.name: Union Culturelle Musulmane
12.text:
The Muslim Cultural Union was founded in Dakar in 1953 by Cheikh Touré, a young scholar inspired by the reformist Islam of the Arab world. It became the leading voice of Islamic reform in French West Africa, and although the regime drew several of its leaders closer in the 1960s, its sections remain active in Dakar and Thiès.

The UCM criticizes the hierarchy and superstitions of the Sufi orders, promotes Arabic and modern Islamic education, and wants Islamic values to shape public life. Influenced by the Muslim Brotherhood, it is anti-colonial and anti-communist, and its base lies among teachers, students and the urban educated.

13.name: Les Technocrates du Palais
13.text:
Senghor governs through a circle of young, French-trained administrators whom he has promoted over the party barons. Its rising star is Abdou Diouf, former secretary-general of the presidency and now minister of planning, whom Senghor is grooming for higher office as he prepares to restore the post of prime minister.

The technocrats believe in efficient central administration, development plans and the gradual Africanization of the civil service, with politics firmly subordinated to the state. Non-aligned in rhetoric but pragmatic in practice, they keep close ties with French and international lenders, and their power lies in drafting the decrees, budgets and plans on which the president depends.

14.name: Tidjaniya
14.text:
The Tijaniyya is Senegal's largest Sufi order by number of followers, divided into rival branches: the Sy family at Tivaouane, led by Khalife Abdoul Aziz Sy; the Niassène branch of Ibrahima Niass at Kaolack, with disciples across West Africa; and the Tall family descended from El Hadj Omar.

Tijani leaders cultivate Islamic learning, pilgrimage and strong ties to the Arab world, and generally rally behind the government in return for patronage. Conservative in morals and wary of secular radicals, they hold the loyalty of townspeople and farmers in Cayor, Saloum and Fouta, and their combined voice weighs heavily in any national crisis.

15.name: Les Maisons de Bordeaux
15.text:
The Bordeaux trading houses, Maurel et Prom, Peyrissac and Devès et Chaumet, together with their larger rivals CFAO and SCOA, have dominated the groundnut trade and import business of Senegal for a century. Independence curtailed their grip through state marketing boards, but they still control much of wholesale trade, credit and shipping.

They lobby for low taxes, free repatriation of profits and the protection of French capital, relying on the Chamber of Commerce, the French embassy and personal ties with ministers. Their influence is resented by African merchants and leftists alike, but no Senegalese government can easily dispense with their credit and networks.

16.name: Chambre de Commerce, d'Industrie et d'Agriculture de Dakar
16.english: Dakar Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture
16.native_full: Chambre de Commerce, d'Industrie et d'Agriculture de Dakar
16.text:
The Dakar Chamber of Commerce, Industry and Agriculture, created in the colonial era, is the official voice of business in the capital. Long run by French and Lebanese firms, it now counts a growing number of Senegalese entrepreneurs who demand their share of the market.

The chamber argues for free enterprise, lower taxes, fewer state monopolies and an investment-friendly climate that keeps foreign capital in Senegal. It is firmly oriented towards France and the European Economic Community, whose association agreements secure Senegal's export markets, and its leverage lies in its role as the government's main partner on economic policy.

17.name: Les Gardiens du Niokolo-Koba
17.text:
The guardians of Niokolo-Koba are the foresters, park rangers and naturalists who protect Senegal's great national park in the southeast, a sanctuary for elephants, lions and chimpanzees. Together with scientists at IFAN and the forestry service they form the country's small conservation lobby.

They warn that the advance of groundnut cultivation, charcoal burning and poaching is destroying forests and wildlife, and demand new reserves, controls on land clearing and protection for the Saloum delta and the Djoudj wetlands. Their influence depends on international partners and on Senghor's concern for Senegal's image abroad.

18.name: Union Progressiste Sénégalaise
18.text:
The Senegalese Progressive Union, which grew out of the Bloc Démocratique Sénégalais founded by Léopold Sédar Senghor in 1948, has ruled Senegal since independence. Having absorbed or banned its rivals, it is the de facto single party, led by President Senghor, who is preparing a constitutional reform to restore the post of prime minister after the crises of 1968 and 1969.

The UPS preaches an African socialism rooted in Négritude, cooperatives and planning, combined with close ties to France, the franc zone and the West. Its strength rests on alliances with the Mouride and Tijani marabouts, rural notables, civil servants and the clans that deliver the vote in every region.

19.name: Les Jeunes Marxistes-Léninistes
19.text:
The young Marxist-Leninists are a clandestine milieu of students, teachers and dissidents who broke with the pro-Soviet African Independence Party in the late 1960s, accusing it of revisionism. Inspired by the Chinese Cultural Revolution and the events of May 1968, they meet in secret cells in Dakar and Saint-Louis and among Senegalese students in France.

They denounce Senghor's regime as a neo-colonial puppet, reject Moscow's peaceful coexistence and call for a people's war rooted in the peasantry. Small and divided, they still circulate underground bulletins, and their influence among students and young teachers gives them weight beyond their numbers.

20.name: Les Commerçants de Sandaga
20.text:
The traders of Sandaga, Dakar's great central market, are the backbone of a Senegalese merchant class squeezed between French firms and Lebanese wholesalers. Many are Mouride disciples whose commercial networks stretch from the groundnut basin to the capital.

They demand the Africanization of commerce, cheap credit for Senegalese businessmen and curbs on 'foreign' merchants and their privileges. Their populism mixes religious conservatism, resentment of state officials and suspicion of intellectuals, and their leverage lies in their ability to close shops, finance politicians and mobilize the brotherhood networks of the city.

21.name: Les Nostalgiques de l'Empire
21.text:
The diehards of empire are a milieu of French settlers, former colonial officials and veterans in Dakar who never accepted decolonization. Some sympathized with the cause of French Algeria and the OAS, and they maintain clubs, veterans' associations and contacts with the French far right.

They despise African self-government, demand the permanence of French bases and privileges, and would welcome a strongman ready to crush unions and students by force. Their numbers are small and shrinking, but their place in business, the security services and among French advisers gives them more reach than their size suggests.

22.name: Forces armées sénégalaises
22.text:
The Senegalese Armed Forces, built from colonial units after independence, are commanded by General Jean Alfred Diallo, the chief of staff who sided with Senghor against Mamadou Dia in 1962. In May 1968 the army occupied Dakar to restore order, confirming its role as the regime's ultimate guarantor.

Trained and equipped by France and backed by French troops stationed near the capital, the forces pride themselves on obedience to civilian authority. Senegal remains free of coups, but the officers' loyalty to Senghor, their ties to Paris and their role in every crisis make them a power in their own right.

23.name: Les Guelowars
23.text:
The Guelowar are the matrilineal royal dynasty that ruled the Serer kingdoms of Sine and Saloum for centuries. Since independence the kings have lost all official power, and with the passing of the last crowned rulers at the end of the 1960s the royal houses survive as lineages, courts and ceremonial titles.

Royalist notables hope to preserve Serer customs, land rights and the dignity of the old kingdoms within the republic. They have no political organization, but their prestige among the Serer peasantry of Sine and Saloum and their ties to village chiefs give them a voice in the regime's rural patronage.
